fields.Q1:
WHAT IS STANDING AROUND THIS ROOM MADE OF?**

At the size shown, **I cannot tell — there is nothing there to put a hand on.** The border is black.

Under an 8× gamma lift it resolves into a smooth pale-grey stone or plaster face, laid in shallow horizontal courses ~10px deep, with a darker skirting course at its foot. But that is a lab answer, not a played one.
fields.Q1_WHY: Raw pixel values. Top band (y 10–170): mean luminance **10.3/255**, 99th percentile **20.3**. Bottom band (y 714–778): mean **10.5**, max **17**. Left column (x 0–66, y 210–700): mean **9.3**, max **21**. The lit floor at y=430 runs **85–185**. The standing structure is delivered at 4–8% luminance across the entire frame. Sampling column x=120 from y=165 to y=211, every pixel is between (2,2,3) and (9,9,11) — wall face, skirting, and floor alike. There is no material information above the noise floor.
fields.Q2:
SOLID MASS, OR A FLAT PATTERN AROUND THE EDGE?**

**Flat pattern.** No hesitation.

The left wall (`c_left`) terminates at x≈55 in a single 2px dark line, and floor tiles begin at x=57. No side face, no top face, no cast shadow onto the floor, no thickness anywhere on the perimeter. The wall foot at the top is one dark row at y=171–174 and then a band of small vertical divisions to y≈202 — a skirting *drawn on*, not a base *seen from above*. The left wall simply stops at y≈430 with no corner, no end-cap, no return.

The decisive proof is the freestanding block at **x 182–248, y 396–462** (one tile, inside the light pool where you can actually see it): the vertical crack glyph on its right side **runs straight across its lower boundary and continues onto the floor below it**. The crack is a decal painted coplanar with the ground. Nothing that stands proud of a floor gets cracked continuously with it.
fields.Q3:
WHERE EXACTLY DOES THE GROUND STOP?**

Two different answers depending on where you look, which is itself the problem.

*Inside the light pool* (x≈270–560, north edge): sampling column x=400 downward, luminance ramps **16.9 (y150) → 22.2 (y170) → 30.9 (y190) → 36.3 (y200) → 46.0 (y218)**. That is a ~50px smear with no edge event in it. The only hard transition is the 4px dark row at **y=171–174**, where value drops 8→2.

*Outside the light pool* (x=120, x=640): **the ground does not stop.** Column x=640 reads 8,8,3,3,3,3… 3,2,4,7 from y=165 to y=211 — a 1–5 value wobble. There is no transition. The room's northern boundary at x<270 and x>560 does not exist as a visible event; it is inferred entirely from the light dying.
fields.Q4:
WHAT IS HOLDING THIS PLACE TOGETHER?**

Almost **NOTHING**, and I want to be precise about the "almost."

There is exactly one piece of visible fastening in the whole frame: a vertical batten with three horizontal cross-bindings at approximately **x 138–152, y 128–172**, on the top wall. It reads as a driven pin or a lashed splint. There are also flat dark plates — **(85–100, 82–93)**, **(60–100, 245–265)** — that could be patches over cracks. Under 8× lift, all of them.

At 1:1, none of it is visible, and even at 8× none of it *is holding anything*. The splint sits beside a crack, not across it. Cut it and nothing moves. No rope spans a gap, no timber props a lintel, no pin passes through two things and joins them. For a place held by four hundred years of orc field repair, the wall is bearing its own weight by assertion.
fields.Q5:
BUILT, OR AN IMAGE THAT WAS REPEATED?**

**Repeated.** Measured, not felt.

Grid pitch is **64px** (horizontal autocorrelation of the top band peaks at 0.582 at lag 64; vertical at 0.358 at lag 64). Correlating gradient maps across all 33 wall tiles, the median pairwise score is 0.154 — and then:

- **(482,714) vs (546,714): 0.975.** Directly adjacent on the bottom wall. Identical zigzag crack, identical forked tail, 64px apart, side by side.
- **(98,714) vs (226,714): 0.937.** Same wall, two tiles apart.
- **(162,10) vs (226,10): 0.822.** Adjacent on the top wall.

In `dup_bottom2` (x 82–306, bottom wall) I count four near-identical zigzags at 64px pitch in a 224px strip. Every crack starts near its cell's top edge and ends near its bottom edge. None crosses a cell seam. This is a stamp, and it is stamped next to itself.
fields.Q6:
WOULD YOU BELIEVE THIS SHIPPED IN A COMMERCIAL GAME?**

**YES.** Plenty of shipped games have unreadable perimeters.

Merely competent, or genuinely good? **Merely competent** — and only when magnified. As delivered on a phone, the walls contribute nothing but the absence of floor. The underlying art is a flat banded field, a repeated crack glyph, three plates and one splint. That is a competent tile set, presented at a brightness where none of it survives.
fields.Q7:
WHAT CAN YOU ACTUALLY SEE ON THE STANDING SURFACES AT 1:1?**

Legible at 1:1: **nothing on the wall face.** Not the courses, not a single crack, not a plate, not the splint, not the skirting, not the wall-foot line. There is a faintly warmer vertical column north of the figure and a small quadrilateral to the west. That is the complete list.

Only under magnification + gamma: horizontal ~10px course banding; vertical zigzag cracks; dark rectangular plates; the bound splint at (138–152, 128–172); the skirting band y 175–202 with its small vertical divisions; a scatter of 1px speckle.

Does it change with distance from the figure? **Barely, and that is the failure.** The wall never enters the light. The closest the standing structure comes to being lit is the northern arc **x≈270–560, y 170–205**, where the face reads **12–35** against floor at **40–100**. That arc gives you an *edge* — you can see the floor stop — but even there the face itself is 5–14% luminance and carries no legible mark. Everywhere else (x<270, x>560, the whole left/right/bottom perimeter) the wall is flat black and does not vary. The light falloff and the wall's own value are indistinguishable.
fields.Q7_WHY: Checked at 1:1 — the full 750×800 frame; the north-gap region (300–520, 0–230); the wall-foot strip (240–600, 140–230); the block at (160–280, 380–490). Had to magnify (4×, plus gamma 0.35 and 0.18) — the top band (0–260, 0–240) for the splint and plates; the bottom band (82–306, 706–782) and (466–626, 706–782) for the duplicate cracks; the left column (0–90, 180–560) for the course banding and wall termination.
fields.Q8:
IS THERE ANYTHING YOUR EYE KEEPS RETURNING TO?**

Three things.

1. **The same crack, four times, on the bottom wall.** The zigzag-with-forked-tail glyph at x=98, 226, 482 and 546 (all y 714–778). Once you see it at 482 and 546 sitting next to each other you cannot unsee the pitch.
2. **Crack position within the cell.** Every crack enters near its cell's top edge and exits near its bottom edge, roughly mid-cell horizontally. Same place in every cell.
3. **The dark rectangular plate blobs.** Roughly 40×18px, at (85,88), (200,105), (330,15), (515,20), (610,40), (650,100) and more. Same size, same aspect, same value, scattered without regard to what they would be patching.
fields.Q9:
WHAT IS BEYOND THE WALLS?**

**Nothing is beyond the walls, because the image contains no beyond.** The frame ends at the outside of the wall band on all four sides — the wall runs to x=0, y=0, y=799 and off the right edge. There is no gap, no void tile, no seam, no darker register outside the structure. The border is the picture's edge.

That means the answer to "is it more of the same, empty space, or another room" is: **unanswerable from the image, and not in a good way.** Not "a dark I cannot name" — an absence of any statement. The wall's outer face and the canvas edge are the same line. Nothing tells me whether this room is one cell of a filing system or the last thing in the world.
fields.Q10:
COULD YOU TELL A WAY THROUGH FROM A DEAD END WITHOUT WALKING INTO IT?**

I found it: **x≈375–440, running from y≈200 up to y=0.** Exactly one 64px tile wide, on-grid.

**No, you could not tell.** At y=100, luminance across it reads: x=350 → 8.3, x=380 → 4.1, x=400 → 8.3, x=430 → 7.3, x=450 → 8.3. The gap is **8.3**. The wall flanking it is **8.3**. Zero contrast. At y=40 the gap is *darker* than the wall to its right. The passage and the stone it passes through are the same value.

What *does* betray it is a warm-hue shift where the corridor floor meets the light pool around y=150–200 — the corridor is faintly warmer than the wall because it is floor. Under gamma lift it reads unambiguously as a passage: two clean wall edges at x=375 and x=440, floor texture continuing north, and the light pool's spill running up it. That is a good passage read at 8× brightness, and no read at all at 1:1. On a phone this is a wall you walk into and discover.
fields.Q11:
HAS ANYTHING HAPPENED TO THIS STRUCTURE?**

Read from the magnified view: it is **cracked, uniformly and decoratively, and otherwise untouched.** Vertical fractures on most cells, a handful of flat plates, one bound splint. No spalling, no missing courses, no slumping, no repair that changes the wall's line, no accumulation at the base, no difference between one stretch of wall and another. The damage is evenly distributed at one cell per crack — which reads as texture, not as history.

Nothing has *happened* to it. Cracks were applied to it. A wall in continuous heavy use since before records, held by soldiers who are extremely good at repair and indifferent to appearance, should be legibly worse in some places than others, and should show at least one repair that is load-bearing and ugly. This one is evenly distressed wallpaper.

---
fields.CULL: Walls render at 4% luminance — invisible at play size, including the only exit north.
fields.FLIP LIST:
- Raise the wall value floor so the perimeter reads at 1:1 in full darkness — the face must separate from the floor by value, not by light falloff, at every distance including the bottom and left edges.
- Give the wall thickness: a distinct top face and a lit inner-edge lip, plus a cast shadow onto the floor, so the boundary is mass and not a colour change.
- Make the north passage at x 375–440 readable at 1:1 — brighten or edge-light the two jambs at x=375 and x=440 so a passage is distinguishable from a notch before you walk into it.
- Break the 64px crack stamp: no two adjacent cells may share a glyph (currently x=482/546 at 0.975 and x=98/226 at 0.937 on the bottom wall), and cracks must cross cell seams.
- Add at least one load-bearing repair that visibly holds something — a pin driven through a split, a timber spanning a break, rope pulling two courses together — and stop decals like the crack at x 182–248 running across the standing block onto the floor.

*Model: Claude Opus 5 (1M context)*
